content: Platelet transfusions are a critical intervention for preventing and managing bleeding in individuals with thrombocytopenia. Despite advancements in donor screening and laboratory testing, there remains a residual risk of viral, bacterial, or protozoal contamination in platelet products. Additionally, newly emerging transfusion-transmitted infections pose a challenge, as laboratory tests may not be available during the initial outbreak. One proposed solution to mitigate these risks is photochemical pathogen reduction, a process that inactivates or significantly reduces the number of pathogens in platelet concentrates. This technique may also extend platelet shelf life and eliminate the need for gamma irradiation of platelets. However, concerns have been raised regarding the efficacy of pathogen-reduced platelets in post-transfusion platelet count recovery and their ability to prevent bleeding compared to standard platelets. This updated Cochrane review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of pathogen-reduced platelets in preventing bleeding in individuals of any age requiring platelet transfusions. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing pathogen-reduced platelets to standard platelets or comparing different types of pathogen-reduced platelets. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, identifying 15 eligible trials, including 12 completed trials with 2075 participants and three ongoing trials. Of the completed trials, 10 were included in the original review. Nine trials compared Intercept® pathogen-reduced platelets to standard platelets, two compared Mirasol® pathogen-reduced platelets to standard platelets, and one compared both types to standard platelets. The trials included both parallel-group and cross-over designs, with most participants being thrombocytopenic individuals with hematological or oncological diagnoses. Only one trial included children undergoing cardiac surgery or adults requiring liver transplantation. The quality of evidence across outcomes ranged from low to high, as assessed using GRADE methodology. The review found low-quality evidence suggesting uncertainty about whether pathogen-reduced platelets increase the risk of any bleeding (WHO Grade 1 to 4). There was no significant difference between pathogen-reduced and standard platelets in the incidence of clinically significant bleeding (WHO Grade 2 or higher) or severe bleeding (WHO Grade 3 or higher), with moderate-quality evidence supporting these findings. Similarly, there was probably no difference in all-cause mortality at 4 to 12 weeks or in the incidence of serious adverse events, based on moderate-quality evidence. Importantly, no bacterial transfusion-transmitted infections were reported in the six trials that assessed this outcome. However, participants who received pathogen-reduced platelets were at a higher risk of developing platelet refractoriness, with high-quality evidence supporting this finding. These participants also required more platelet transfusions and had shorter intervals between transfusions, with highand moderate-quality evidence, respectively. Additionally, pathogen-reduced platelets were associated with a lower 24-hour corrected count increment, indicating reduced efficacy in increasing platelet counts post-transfusion. None of the included studies reported on quality of life or economic outcomes. Subgroup analyses revealed differences between the two pathogen-reduction technologies (Intercept® and Mirasol®) in terms of all-cause mortality and the interval between transfusions, with Intercept® showing more favorable outcomes. The authors concluded that in individuals with hematological or oncological disorders who are thrombocytopenic due to their disease or its treatment, pathogen-reduced platelets increase the risk of platelet refractoriness and the need for additional transfusions. However, they do not appear to affect all-cause mortality, the risk of clinically significant or severe bleeding, or the risk of serious adverse events. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions for individuals with other diagnoses. Three ongoing trials are expected to provide further insights, focusing on adults with hematological or oncological conditions.
